The lesions gradually increased in size with subsequent central ulceration and blackish crusting. No fever, pain, or discharge from the lesions was noted. Patient had history of kidney transplant in 2004 causing immunocompromised status.

Two distinct lesions measuring 2 × 2 cm each were identified over the glabella and right cheek. The lesions were firm with central ulceration with hemorrhagic crusting. Dermoscopy showed arborizing telangiectasias, central ulceration with crusting, and peripheral pigment. No additional lesions or abnormalities were found on examination of surrounding skin and general systemic evaluation.

- Histopathological examination:    Image Title: Figure 1B    Image Description: Extensive dermal collection of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and macrophages. Intracellular yeasts with surrounding halos were identified (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×40)      - Molecular Testing:    Polymerase chain reaction analysis of tissue specimen was performed      - Imaging Studies:    Computed tomography of chest and abdomen showed no involvement of internal organs      - Clinical Photography:    Image Title: Figure 1A    Image Description: Two distinct, well-defined, umbilicated skin-colored lesions measuring 2 × 2 cm each located over the glabella and right cheek with central ulceration and hemorrhagic crusting

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Cutaneous histoplasmosis
B. Cutaneous cryptococcosis
C. Histoplasmosis
D. Cutaneous blastomycosis

response.rationale: The presence of intracellular yeasts with prominent surrounding halos on histology, combined with an immunocompromised transplant recipient, is highly specific for Cryptococcus. Histoplasmosis typically shows smaller intracellular yeasts without such halos, and blastomycosis features broad-based budding, not halos. The cutaneous-only presentation and lack of systemic involvement further support a primary cutaneous cryptococcal infection.

There was more extensive bilateral FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes and periventricular white matter and progression of the spinal cord lesions.

input_text:
An 8-year-old, previously healthy, fully immunized girl presented with 5 days of intermittent fever followed by abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had been at home due to the COVID-19 pandemic; her parents had mild upper respiratory symptoms for 1 week. Outpatient oral antibiotics and IV fluids did not improve her symptoms. She was admitted to surgery with suspected appendicitis; abdominal ultrasonography was normal. Persistent fever, abdominal pain, and the emergence of a rash and conjunctivitis prompted transfer to the pediatric COVID-19 ward. 

On examination, temperature was 38.6 °C. She had bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, erythematous throat, palmar erythema, a strawberry tongue, and an erythema multiforme–type rash; there was no hypotension, lymphadenopathy, or respiratory distress. Cardiac examination revealed a grade II/VI murmur at the left sternal border; lung sounds were normal.

Laboratory tests showed ESR 67 mm/h, CRP 166 mg/L, platelet count 192×10^9/L, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, and WBC 10.3×10^9/L with 82% neutrophils. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Urinalysis and urine culture were negative. A high-resolution chest CT scan was not indicative of COVID-19. Reverse transcription PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and blood cultures were negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Kawasaki disease
B. appendicitis
C. Suspected appendicitis
D. Acute COVID
E. Toxic shock syndrome
F. Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS
G. Macrophage activation syndrome/hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (MAS/HLH)
H. Classic Kawasaki disease

response.rationale: MIS-C is favored by the combination of prolonged fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, mucocutaneous findings, and marked inflammation in a child with COVID-19 exposure, despite negative PCR. A 27-year-old woman who works as an agricultural laborer was referred with fatigue, malaise, anorexia, and epistaxis. On examination, she was pale, with eczematous plaques on her chest and proximal right arm, and had splenomegaly 6 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, white-cell count 4.0×10^9/L, and platelets 23×10^9/L. A peripheral-blood smear revealed lymphoblasts. Flow cytometry was positive for TdT, CD34, CD19, CD10, CD22, and HLA-DR, and bone marrow evaluation confirmed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The eczematous plaques were treated as contact dermatitis with topical methylprednisolone, resolving rapidly, and induction chemotherapy with hyper-CVAD was initiated. 

On day 8, she developed febrile neutropenia and received piperacillin–tazobactam. Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species grew in blood cultures, prompting addition of teicoplanin. Persistent fever led to repeat cultures, which grew Enterococcus species, and teicoplanin was replaced with daptomycin. High-resolution chest CT showed nonspecific nodules under 1 cm, and serum galactomannan antigen was negative. After 10 days of fever with an absolute neutrophil count of 20/μL, she reported severe pain in her right arm radiating to her shoulder, suggesting herpes zoster; however, no vesicles were present. On examination, there was a very tender point in the upper lateral scapular region with an underlying vague mass. MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated a focal cystic necrotic lesion between the teres minor and teres major muscles.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Mucormycosis
B. Herpes zoster considered because of dermatomal pain distribution
C. Bacterial infection considered due to febrile neutropenia and positive blood cultures
